newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa Sacob sees GDP slowing to 2.3 pct in '97.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa Sacob sees GDP slowing to 2.3 pct in '97.

text.p: South Africa's economic growth rate was expected to slow to 2.3 percent next year from an expected 3.0 percent in 1996, the South African Chamber of Business said on Thursday.

"While Sacob's forecast growth for 1997 at 2.3 percent is lower than the three percent forecast for 1996, present evidence suggests that the economy can achieve a soft landing in 1997," the chamber's director of economic policy Ben van Rensburg told reporters.
Sacob director-general Raymond Parsons said despite the expected soft landing it would still be a tough year for business and consumers.

"The incidence of household debt, interest rates, slow rise in money wages, and higher inflation will put a squeeze on the average consumer and business person. Inflation is expected to average nine percent next year," Parsons said.
Although the economy would slow down next year, it would also be a period of consolidation, he said.
"The foundations have to be laid to take full advantage of the next economic upturn by putting the right policies in place."
Parson said that lessons from the past had shown the country's maximum growth achievement was three percent, hemmed in by inflation and the balance of payments.
"South Africa has to break out of this low growth trap -- and GEAR (Growth, Employment and Redistribution strategy) offers the basic way in which to do so," Parsons said.

Key aspects of GEAR -- government's five-year economic plan -- were the liberalisation of markets which would lead to the lifting of exchange controls, labour market flexibility and privatisation, he said.

He said the deficits in the balance of payments and on the budget looked promising. A reduction in the trade deficit and meeting four percent deficit before borrowing in the Budget next year should contribute to financial stability, Parsons said.
He said South Africa should also exploit the positive outlook for the world economy next year.
Parsons was speaking at the release of the chamber's monthly business confidence index, which fell to 111.3 in November from 114.3 in October.

Sacob said the major reasons for the fall in the index included the anti-cyclical rise in the Bank rate in November, higher short-term interest rates after the rate hike, the weaker gold price and higher fuel prices.
Another factor was the higher inflation rate. Latest year-on-year figures show October CPI at 9.1 percent versus 8.4 in September. Inflation in 1997 was expected to average 9.0 percent, Sacob said.

Commenting on the surprise surge in exports in October, which boosted that month's trade surplus to 3.9 billion rand, Sacob said it expected exports would grow faster than imports in 1997, resulting in a narrowing of the current account deficit.
